gams

Splines

  • Piecewise regression yields continuous functions which are not, generally, smooth. Regression with splines yields smooth continuous functions.

  • A spline is essentially a Piecewise Polynomial but force the ends of these pieces to meet perfectly smoothly so it looks like one continuous line.

  • A “spline” was a flexible strip of wood used by draftsmen to draw smooth curves through a set of points. We will do the same with several simple polynomial segments at specific points called knots

knots

We break the \(x\)-axis into smaller regions. The specific points where we divide these regions are called knots.

Inside each region (between two knots), we fit a simple polynomial, usually a cubic (degree 3) function.

We must connect or touch each polynomial at the knot. Further, they must be smooth, non jerky transitions.

Code 
# Load necessary libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# --- 1. Generate Synthetic Data ---
set.seed(123) # Ensures the data is the same every time
n_points <- 100
x <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = n_points)
# Create a sine-wave pattern with some noise, similar to the example image
y <- sin(x / 1.5) * 1.5 + rnorm(n_points, sd = 0.3)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# --- 2. Define Knots and Calculate Piecewise Averages ---
# Define the locations of the vertical "knots"
knots <- c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10)

# Create a data frame for the segments.
# We determine the start/end x-coordinates and calculate the mean y-value for each bin.
segments_df <- data.frame(
  x_start = knots[-length(knots)], # Starts of the intervals
  x_end = knots[-1],               # Ends of the intervals
  bin_id = factor(1:(length(knots) - 1)) # ID for coloring
)

# Calculate the mean y-value within each interval
segments_df$y_mean <- apply(segments_df, 1, function(row) {
  x_s <- as.numeric(row["x_start"])
  x_e <- as.numeric(row["x_end"])
  
  # Filter data within the knot interval. 
  # Use x < x_e to avoid double-counting, but include it for the last segment.
  if (x_e == max(knots)) {
    in_bin <- df$x >= x_s & df$x <= x_e
  } else {
    in_bin <- df$x >= x_s & df$x < x_e
  }
  mean(df$y[in_bin], na.rm = TRUE)
})

# Define custom colors to match the example image roughly
segment_colors <- c("#377eb8", "#ff7f00", "#4daf4a", "#e41a1c")


# --- 3. Create the Plot ---
ggplot() +
  # Layer 1: The data points
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "black", size = 2) +
  
  # Layer 2: The vertical dashed lines for knots
  # We map linetype to a static string to create a legend entry
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = knots, linetype = "Knot"), 
             color = "gray50", size = 0.8) +
  
  # Layer 3: The horizontal piecewise average lines
  geom_segment(data = segments_df, 
               aes(x = x_start, xend = x_end, 
                   y = y_mean, yend = y_mean, 
                   color = bin_id), 
               size = 1.5) +
  
  # --- Customization for styling ---
  scale_color_manual(values = segment_colors, guide = "none") + # Manually set colors and hide segment legend
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "", values = c("Knot" = "dashed")) + # Configure the knot legend
  
  # Set plot limits and labels
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-10, 10, 5), limits = c(-10.5, 10.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-2, 1, 1), limits = c(-2.2, 1.8)) +
  labs(title = "Piecewise constant", x = "x", y = "y") +
  
  # Apply a clean theme and customize font sizes
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.position = c(0.85, 0.5), # Place legend inside the plot
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"), # Make legend line longer
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(splines) # Essential package for GAMs/Splines

# --- 1. Setup Data (Same as before) ---
set.seed(123)
n_points <- 100
x <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = n_points)
y <- sin(x / 1.5) * 1.5 + rnorm(n_points, sd = 0.3)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Define Knots
# Note: For splines, we distinguish between "Boundary" knots (ends) and "Interior" knots (middle)
knots_all <- c(-10, -5, 0, 5, 10) 
knots_interior <- c(-5, 0, 5)

# --- 2. Fit the Spline Models ---

# Model A: Linear Spline (Degree 1)
# "bs" stands for B-Spline basis. Degree 1 = Linear lines connected at knots.
fit_linear <- lm(y ~ bs(x, knots = knots_interior, degree = 1), data = df)
df$pred_linear <- predict(fit_linear, newdata = df)

# Model B: Cubic Spline (Degree 3)
# Degree 3 = Cubic curves connected smoothly at knots.
fit_cubic <- lm(y ~ bs(x, knots = knots_interior, degree = 3), data = df)
df$pred_cubic <- predict(fit_cubic, newdata = df)

# --- 3. Plotting Functions ---

# Helper to create the base plot style
create_spline_plot <- function(data, y_col, title, line_color) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    # Raw Data
    geom_point(color = "black", size = 2) +
    
    # Knots (Vertical Lines)
    geom_vline(xintercept = knots_all, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
    
    # The Spline Fit
    geom_line(aes_string(y = y_col), color = line_color, size = 1.5) +
    
    # Styling
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = knots_all, limits = c(-10.5, 10.5)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = "Vertical dashed lines = Knots") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14),
      axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# --- 4. Generate the Two Figures ---

# Figure 1: Linear Spline (Piecewise Linear)
# Notice: It has sharp "elbows" at the knots. It is Continuous but not Smooth.
plot_linear <- create_spline_plot(df, "pred_linear", "Linear Spline (Degree 1)", "#377eb8")
print(plot_linear)

B-splines (from bell shaped due to the cubic nature)
::: {.cell}
{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} plot_cubic <- create_spline_plot(df, "pred_cubic", "Cubic Spline (Degree 3)", "#e41a1c") print(plot_cubic)

## Basis Functions
\[f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \cdot B_j(x)\]
- Splines have Local effects rather than polynomials where the curve is across the entire range of X. To fit these local curves inbetween knots, we need to create a series of basis functions to essential turn on and off the effect at different values of X.

Basis functions. We are describing many different “hills” for each value of x via how many knots.

How much does this specific hill overlap with this specific data point? Peak or down the hill a little

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(splines)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(123)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(100, sd = 0.2)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

basis_matrix <- bs(x, df = 6, intercept = TRUE)

The matrix is unpacked, much like a categorical variable into a dummy. You get something like: y ~ Column1 + Column2 + Column3 + Column4 + Column5 + Column6

Tells us how tall each hill is.

Code 
model <- lm(y ~ 0 + basis_matrix) 
coeffs <- coef(model)
summary(model)

lm(formula = y ~ 0 + basis_matrix)

B is the basis and tells us where the hills are.

\(\beta_j\) tells us how tall the hills are (weights)

Multiplying together tells us the Weighted shapes

\[f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \cdot B_j(x)\]

Code 
scaled_basis <- basis_matrix %*% diag(coeffs)
basis_df <- as.data.frame(scaled_basis)
basis_df$x <- x
basis_df$Total_Curve <- rowSums(scaled_basis) 

basis_long <- basis_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("V"), names_to = "Basis_Function", values_to = "Value")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, fill = Basis_Function), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = basis_df, aes(x = x, y = Total_Curve), 
            color = "black", size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
  labs(title = "Anatomy of a Spline",
       subtitle = "Colored Areas = Weighted Basis Functions \nBlack Line = The Combination ",
       y = "Y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

4 knots

Code 
set.seed(123)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(100, sd = 0.2)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
basis_matrix <- bs(x, df = 4, intercept = TRUE) 
model <- lm(y ~ basis_matrix - 1) 
coeffs <- coef(model)
scaled_basis <- basis_matrix %*% diag(coeffs)
basis_df <- as.data.frame(scaled_basis)
basis_df$x <- x
basis_df$Total_Curve <- rowSums(scaled_basis) 
basis_long <- basis_df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("V"), names_to = "Basis_Function", values_to = "Value")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_area(data = basis_long, aes(x = x, y = Value, fill = Basis_Function), 
            alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = basis_df, aes(x = x, y = Total_Curve), 
            color = "black", size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

GAMs

  • Offer a solution to the regression spline issue of how many knots should we fit by utilizing penalized (regularized) splines. Plus more!

  • GAMs offer a middle ground from simple lines to localized lowess curves: they can be fit to complex, nonlinear relationships and make good predictions in these cases, but we are still able to do inferential statistics and understand and explain the underlying structure of our models

Generalized additive models

Similar to going from general linear model to generalized linear model. One more generalization.

\[y \sim ExpoFam(\mu, etc.)\] \[E(y) = \mu\]

\[g(\mu) = b_0 + f(x_1) + f(x_2) \;...\;+f(x_p)\]

The key difference is that the linear predictor now incorporates smooth functions of at least some (possibly all) features, represented as f(x), and this will allow for nonlinear relationships between the features and the target variable y.

Cherry blossom data

Code 
library(rethinking)
data(cherry_blossoms)
d <- cherry_blossoms
rm(cherry_blossoms)
detach(package:rethinking, unload = T)

d %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = doy)) +
  geom_point(color = "#ffb7c5", alpha = 1/2) +
  theme_bw() +
    theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#4f455c"),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

\[f(x) = w_1 B_{i, 1} + w_2 B_{i, 2} + w_3 B_{i, 3} + \dots\]

  • B-splines invent a series of entirely new, synthetic predictor variables. The hills. Each of these synthetic variables exists only to gradually turn a specific parameter on and off within a specific range of the real predictor variable.

  • Each of the synthetic variables is called a basis function and serve as weights

knots

Code 
d2 <-
  d %>% 
  drop_na(doy)

num_knots <- 15
knot_list <- quantile(d2$year, probs = seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = num_knots))

d %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = doy)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = knot_list, color = "white", alpha = 1/2) +
  geom_point(color = "#ffb7c5", alpha = 1/2) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#4f455c"),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

Basis function

The B column is a matrix column, which contains the same number of rows as the others, but also smuggled in 17 columns within that column. Each of those 17 columns corresponds to one of our synthetic variables.

y ~ b as opposed to y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 …..

estimation

spline <- 
  brm(data = d3,
      family = gaussian,
      doy ~ 1 + B,
      prior = c(prior(normal(100, 10), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      seed = 4,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "spline")

The parameter estimates are very difficult to interpret directly. It’s often easier to just plot the results

Penalized estimation

  • One concern is that we overfit our data and make our lines too wiggly. We can overcome this via penalized estimation, basically balancing minimizing residuals with out of sample prediction.

  • This is what is used in lasso or ridge regression or many other machine learning algorithms.

  • A penalization parameter often called lambda uses cross validation to balance over vs under fitting
